sb-intro-001.explanation: **The problem:** Plain Spring is flexible but verbose — you wire a DispatcherServlet, view resolvers, data sources, and transaction managers by hand (historically in XML). Getting a trivial web app running took a lot of ceremony. **What Spring Boot adds:** (1) **auto-configuration** — it inspects the classpath and configures sensible defaults (see a JDBC driver? configure a DataSource); (2) **starters** — `spring-boot-starter-web` and friends bundle compatible dependencies so you don't version-align them; (3) an **embedded server** so the app is a runnable `java -jar` instead of a WAR deployed to an external Tomcat; (4) **Actuator** for production health/metrics. **The mental model:** Boot is *opinionated* Spring — it makes choices for you and lets you override any of them. **Common misconception:** Boot is not a different framework; it's Spring with batteries included.

resources.label: Spring Boot — Reference: Introducing Spring Boot

sb-intro-002.explanation: **The core idea:** With Inversion of Control, your objects don't construct their own dependencies — the framework does. You hand control of object creation and lifecycle to the Spring **container**. **Dependency Injection** is the concrete technique: a class declares what it needs (usually as constructor parameters) and the container supplies matching beans. **Why it matters:** code depends on *interfaces*, not concrete classes, so you can swap implementations and inject mocks in tests without touching the class. **How Spring does it:** classes annotated `@Component`/`@Service`/etc. become beans; the container resolves the dependency graph and injects instances. **Common mistake:** calling `new MyService()` inside a bean — that object is *not* managed by Spring, so its own `@Autowired`/`@Transactional` annotations won't work.

sb-intro-003.explanation: **What it is:** The `ApplicationContext` is the running IoC container — the in-memory graph of every bean Spring manages. **What it does:** reads your configuration (annotated components, `@Configuration` classes), instantiates beans, injects their dependencies, manages scope and lifecycle callbacks, publishes/handles events, and resolves messages/resources. **How you get one:** `SpringApplication.run()` creates and returns it; in tests `@SpringBootTest` builds one for you. **Relationship to BeanFactory:** `ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory` with enterprise features (events, i18n, eager singleton instantiation at startup). **Practical note:** you rarely call it directly — you let it inject what you need. But understanding that 'the context' *is* your app's object graph explains startup order, scopes, and why a bean must be in the context to be injected.

sb-intro-mcq-001.explanation: **What it bundles:** `@SpringBootApplication` is a meta-annotation combining three: **`@SpringBootConfiguration`** (a specialized `@Configuration`, marking this as a source of bean definitions), **`@EnableAutoConfiguration`** (turns on classpath-driven auto-configuration), and **`@ComponentScan`** (scans this class's package and below for `@Component`/`@Service`/`@Controller`/etc.). **Why it's combined:** these three appear together in virtually every Boot app, so one annotation is cleaner. **Why placement matters:** because `@ComponentScan` defaults to the annotated class's package, the main class should sit in a **root package** above all your code, or components elsewhere won't be discovered. **When you'd split them:** rarely — if you need to customize scan packages or exclude auto-configs, you use the attributes of `@SpringBootApplication` rather than abandoning it.

sb-intro-004.explanation: **The problem it solves:** Building a Spring web app by hand means picking Spring MVC, a JSON library, a validation library, an embedded server, and aligning all their versions. A starter does that for you. **What a starter is:** a dependency descriptor — an artifact that pulls in a curated, version-compatible set of libraries. `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Spring MVC + Jackson + validation + embedded Tomcat. **Naming convention:** official starters are `spring-boot-starter-*`; third-party ones put their name first (`mybatis-spring-boot-starter`). **Key detail:** you usually add a starter *without a version*, because the parent POM / dependencies BOM manages versions. **Common starters:** `-web`, `-data-jpa`, `-security`, `-validation`, `-actuator`, `-test`. **Misconception:** starters contain little or no code — they're about dependencies, not features.
sb-intro-004.example:
```xml
<!-- pom.xml — note: no <version> on the starters; the parent manages them. -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.3.0</version>
</parent>

<dependencies>
    <!-- Pulls in Spring MVC, Jackson, validation, embedded Tomcat -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
    <!-- Test starter: JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ, Spring Test -->
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
        <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

sb-di-001.explanation: **The shared behavior:** all four annotations are detected by component scanning and register the class as a Spring bean. **The differences are about intent (and a little behavior):** `@Component` is the generic stereotype. `@Service` marks the business-logic layer — semantically distinct but behaviorally the same as `@Component`. `@Repository` marks data-access classes and **adds real behavior**: Spring wraps the bean so persistence exceptions are translated into Spring's consistent `DataAccessException` hierarchy. `@Controller` (and `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`) marks web request handlers and is treated specially by Spring MVC. **Why use the specific one:** it documents the layer, lets aspects/tooling target a layer, and (for `@Repository`) gives you exception translation. **Common mistake:** expecting `@Service` to do something magical — for plain bean registration it's identical to `@Component`.

resources.label: Spring — Classpath Scanning and Managed Components

sb-di-002.explanation: **Why constructor injection wins:** (1) **Immutability** — dependencies can be `final`, so a bean can't be left half-built or mutated. (2) **Required by construction** — you literally can't create the object without its dependencies, so a missing one fails fast and visibly. (3) **Testability** — you instantiate with `new Service(mockA, mockB)` in a plain unit test; no Spring, no reflection. (4) **Honest design** — a constructor with eight parameters screams 'this class does too much', whereas field injection hides that smell. **Field injection downsides:** can't be `final`, needs reflection/Spring to set, and easily accumulates hidden dependencies. **Modern convenience:** since Spring 4.3, a single-constructor class needs no `@Autowired`. **Setter injection** has a narrow niche: genuinely optional dependencies. **Rule of thumb:** constructor-inject required deps; that's the community and Spring-team recommendation.

resources.label: Spring Blog — Why field injection is evil (community)

sb-di-003.explanation: **What it does:** `@Autowired` marks an injection point where Spring should supply a matching bean. **Resolution order:** by **type** first; if more than one bean matches, Spring tries to match the field/parameter **name** to a bean name; if still ambiguous, you need `@Qualifier` or `@Primary` or it fails at startup. **Where it goes:** constructor, setter, or field. **The optional rule:** on a class's **single constructor**, `@Autowired` is unnecessary (Spring 4.3+) — Spring autowires automatically. **Optional dependencies:** `@Autowired(required = false)`, or declare the field/parameter as `Optional<T>` or `@Nullable`. **Common mistake:** putting `@Autowired` on a field and wondering why it's `null` in a `new`-constructed object — Spring only injects beans it manages.

sb-di-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer — singleton:** by default Spring creates exactly one instance of each bean *per container* and injects that same instance everywhere. **Why singleton:** most beans (services, repositories, controllers) are stateless behavior holders — sharing one instance is efficient and correct. **The consequence:** because the instance is shared across threads, a singleton bean must be **stateless or thread-safe**. Storing per-request mutable state in a singleton field is a classic concurrency bug. **The other scopes:** `prototype` — a new instance every time the bean is requested; `request` / `session` / `application` — web-aware scopes tied to an HTTP request/session/servlet-context. **Note:** Spring's 'singleton' is one-per-container, not the GoF one-per-JVM singleton.

sb-di-004.explanation: **singleton (default):** one instance per container, created eagerly at startup, lifecycle fully managed by Spring (including destruction callbacks). Must be thread-safe. **prototype:** a brand-new instance every time the bean is requested or injected; Spring creates and hands it off but does **not** manage its destruction — the caller is responsible for cleanup. **The classic gotcha:** inject a prototype bean into a singleton and you get *one* prototype instance, captured when the singleton was built — it never refreshes. **Fixes for 'fresh prototype each time':** (1) inject `ObjectProvider<T>`/`Provider<T>` and call `.getObject()` per use; (2) method injection with `@Lookup`; (3) `@Scope(value = "prototype", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)` so a proxy fetches a new instance per call. **Why people hit it:** the dependency graph is wired once at startup, so a plain field can't 'know' to re-create.

resources.label: Spring — Singleton beans with prototype-bean dependencies

sb-di-005.explanation: **When component scanning isn't enough:** `@Component` only works on classes *you* can annotate. To register a bean from a third-party library (e.g. a `RestClient`, an `ObjectMapper`, a `DataSource`) or one that needs custom construction, you write a `@Bean` method in a `@Configuration` class. **How `@Bean` works:** the method's return value is registered as a bean; the method name is the default bean name; its parameters are injected by the container. **The proxy detail:** `@Configuration` classes are CGLIB-proxied so that calling one `@Bean` method from another returns the *same managed singleton*, not a new object. In 'lite mode' (a `@Bean` method on a plain `@Component`), no such proxying happens and inter-method calls create new instances. **Rule of thumb:** your own classes → `@Component`; things you construct or don't own → `@Bean` in `@Configuration`.

sb-di-006.explanation: **The situation:** when two or more beans satisfy the same type, type-based autowiring is ambiguous and Spring fails at startup with `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`. **Two tools:** **`@Primary`** marks one bean as the default winner whenever the type alone is ambiguous — good when there's an obvious default with rare overrides. **`@Qualifier("name")`** at the injection point names the exact bean to use — explicit, per-injection. **Precedence:** a `@Qualifier` at the injection point overrides `@Primary`. **Custom qualifiers:** you can define your own annotation meta-annotated with `@Qualifier` for type-safe selection (no string literals). **Also:** ask for `List<T>`/`Map<String,T>` to inject *all* matching beans deliberately. **Common mistake:** forgetting that the parameter/field *name* can itself act as a fallback qualifier (it matches a bean name).

sb-di-mcq-002.explanation: **Why it fails fast:** Spring autowires by type. When two `PaymentGateway` beans match and there's no `@Primary` to break the tie and no `@Qualifier`/name match at the injection point, the container cannot choose — and it refuses to guess. So it throws **`NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`** during context startup. **Why fail-fast is good:** an ambiguous wiring caught at boot is far better than silently picking the wrong gateway in production. **How to fix:** mark one bean `@Primary`, or add `@Qualifier("...")` at the injection point, or rename so the parameter name matches a bean name. **The exception — collections:** if you instead declare `List<PaymentGateway>` or `Map<String, PaymentGateway>`, Spring injects *all* matching beans on purpose; that's not ambiguous. **Distractor traps:** Spring does not 'pick the first' or inject `null` for a required single-type dependency.

sb-auto-001.explanation: **The mechanism:** `@EnableAutoConfiguration` (inside `@SpringBootApplication`) loads a registry of auto-configuration classes listed in each jar's `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports` file. **Each is conditional:** every auto-config class is guarded by `@Conditional` annotations — `@ConditionalOnClass` (a type is on the classpath), `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` (you haven't defined your own), `@ConditionalOnProperty` (a flag is set), etc. So a config only applies when it's relevant. **The 'back off' principle:** `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` means auto-config provides a default *only if you didn't*. Define your own `DataSource` and Boot's default quietly steps aside. **Why it feels magical but isn't:** it's just conditional bean registration driven by the classpath + your config. **Debugging:** run with `--debug` to print the **auto-configuration report** showing which configs matched and which didn't (and the precise condition that failed).

resources.label: Spring Boot — Creating Your Own Auto-configuration

sb-auto-002.explanation: **The building blocks of auto-config:** **`@ConditionalOnClass`** — register only if a given class is on the classpath (e.g. configure JPA only if Hibernate is present). **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`** — register only if no bean of that type already exists, which is how auto-config 'backs off' and lets your explicit bean win. **`@ConditionalOnProperty`** — register only when a property has a given value (feature flags). **The negatives:** `@ConditionalOnMissingClass`, `@ConditionalOnBean`, plus `@ConditionalOnWebApplication`, `@ConditionalOnExpression`. **Why this design:** it makes configuration reactive — adding a library or flipping a property changes wiring without code edits. **Where you use them:** mostly inside library/auto-config code, but they're handy in your own `@Configuration` for optional features. **Mistake to avoid:** ordering — conditions evaluate against the bean definitions known at that point, so `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` relies on user config being processed first (Boot handles this ordering for auto-config).

sb-auto-003.explanation: **Why exclude:** sometimes a starter drags in an auto-config you don't want — e.g. `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` triggers `DataSourceAutoConfiguration`, which fails at boot if no database URL is configured and you're not ready for one. **Two ways to exclude:** (1) `@SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)` in code; (2) the `spring.autoconfigure.exclude` property (a list) in `application.properties`/`yml` — handy when you can't edit the annotation. **Diagnose first:** run with `--debug` (or set `debug=true`) to print the **auto-configuration report** — it lists positive matches, negative matches, and exactly which condition each one passed or failed. That tells you the precise class name to exclude. **Caution:** excluding an auto-config also removes the beans it would have created — make sure nothing else depends on them, or provide replacements.

resources.label: Spring Boot — Disabling Specific Auto-configuration Classes

sb-auto-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer:** `@ComponentScan` (composed into `@SpringBootApplication`) defaults to scanning the **package of the annotated main class and all sub-packages**, recursively. **Practical consequence:** put your main application class in a **root/top-level package** (e.g. `com.example`) above all feature packages. Components in a *parent* package or a *sibling* tree that isn't under the main class's package won't be discovered. **The classic bug:** a `@Service` in `com.other` while the main class is in `com.example` → bean never registered → `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at injection. **How to widen the scan:** `@SpringBootApplication(scanBasePackages = {"com.example", "com.shared"})`. **Why not scan everything:** scanning the whole classpath would be slow and would pick up beans from libraries you didn't intend to manage.

resources.label: Spring Boot — Locating the Main Application Class

sb-auto-004.explanation: **The pain it removes:** a Spring app pulls in dozens of transitive libraries (Spring modules, Jackson, Hibernate, Logback, Tomcat). Picking individually compatible versions is error-prone — mismatches cause `NoSuchMethodError` and subtle bugs. **The solution — dependency management:** `spring-boot-starter-parent` (or importing the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM) declares a curated set of versions tested to work together. Your build inherits them, so you list artifacts **without versions**. **How to override a managed version:** set the documented property (e.g. `<jackson-bom.version>2.17.0</jackson-bom.version>` in Maven, or `ext['jackson.version']` in Gradle) — don't just declare an explicit version blindly, as that can desync the whole BOM. **Gradle equivalent:** the `io.spring.dependency-management` plugin or the Spring Boot Gradle plugin imports the same BOM. **Net effect:** consistent, upgrade-in-one-place dependency versions.
sb-auto-004.example:
```xml
<!-- Inherit Boot's curated versions via the parent POM -->
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.3.0</version>
</parent>

<properties>
    <!-- Override a single managed version the SAFE way: via the documented property -->
    <jackson-bom.version>2.17.1</jackson-bom.version>
</properties>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
        <!-- no <version>: managed by the parent -->
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

sb-config-001.explanation: **Where config comes from:** Spring Boot reads `application.properties` or `application.yml` from `src/main/resources` (and a few other locations). But that's just one layer. **The full precedence (low → high):** built-in defaults < `application.properties`/`yml` < profile-specific files (`application-<profile>.yml`) < OS environment variables < JVM system properties (`-D`) < command-line args (`--key=value`) — and a few more (Config Data imports, test properties). Higher layers override lower ones. **Properties vs YAML:** equivalent; YAML is better for nested structures and lists, but can't be loaded via `@PropertySource` and is whitespace-sensitive. **Why the layering matters:** it's what makes one immutable jar deployable everywhere — bake defaults into the file, override the environment-specific bits via env vars at deploy time. **Relaxed binding:** `app.page-size`, `app.pageSize`, and `APP_PAGE_SIZE` all bind to the same property.
sb-config-001.example:
```yaml
# src/main/resources/application.yml
server:
  port: 8080            # default; overridden by SERVER_PORT or --server.port

app:
  page-size: 25         # relaxed binding: APP_PAGE_SIZE env var also maps here
  features:
    - search
    - export

---
# Profile-specific block (activated by spring.profiles.active=prod)
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: prod
server:
  port: 80
```

sb-config-002.explanation: **What it does:** `@Value` injects a single property value into a field or parameter at bean creation. **The default syntax:** `@Value("${app.timeout:30}")` reads property `app.timeout`; the part after the colon (`30`) is the fallback used when the property is absent. Without a default and a missing property, the context fails to start. **Type conversion:** Spring converts the String to the target type (int, boolean, Duration, List via comma-splitting, etc.). **SpEL:** `@Value` also evaluates Spring Expression Language — `@Value("#{systemProperties['user.region']}")`. **When to prefer it:** one-off scalar values. **When NOT to:** groups of related properties or nested structures — use `@ConfigurationProperties` for type-safety, validation, and relaxed binding instead. **Common mistake:** confusing `${...}` (property placeholder) with `#{...}` (SpEL) — they're different resolvers.

sb-config-003.explanation: **The problem with many `@Value`s:** scattering `@Value("${...}")` across classes is stringly-typed, repetitive, and can't validate or bind nested structures. **The solution:** `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app")` binds a whole subtree of properties onto a typed POJO in one shot — including nested objects, lists, and maps. **Benefits:** (1) **type safety** — fields are real types; (2) **relaxed binding** — `app.page-size`, `app.pageSize`, `APP_PAGE_SIZE` all match `pageSize`; (3) **validation** — add `@Validated` + Bean Validation constraints; (4) **centralization** — all related config in one class with IDE/metadata support. **How to enable:** annotate the class and either add `@EnableConfigurationProperties(AppProps.class)` or annotate it `@ConfigurationProperties` + `@Component`, or use constructor binding with `@ConfigurationProperties` on a record/immutable class. **Rule of thumb:** more than a couple of related keys → `@ConfigurationProperties`.

sb-config-004.explanation: **What profiles are for:** segmenting beans and configuration per environment (dev / test / prod) without code branches. **Two halves:** (1) **`@Profile("dev")`** on a `@Component`/`@Bean` — that bean is registered only when the profile is active; a bean with no `@Profile` is always active. (2) **Profile-specific property files** — `application-dev.yml` / `application-prod.yml` are layered on top of the base `application.yml` when their profile is active. **Activation:** `spring.profiles.active=dev` via the property, the env var `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`, or `--spring.profiles.active=dev`. You can activate several at once (comma-separated). **Typical use:** dev profile → in-memory H2 + verbose logging; prod profile → real DB + INFO logging. **Gotcha:** if no profile is active, only the 'default' profile beans + base properties apply; don't rely on a profile being set unless you set it. **Profile groups** let one name activate several.

sb-config-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer — 7070, the command-line argument wins.** **The precedence (highest first, abbreviated):** command-line args (`--key=value`) > JVM system properties (`-Dkey=value`) > OS environment variables > `application-<profile>.properties` > `application.properties` > defaults. So `--server.port=7070` beats `SERVER_PORT=9090` beats the file's `8080`. **Why this order exists:** the most *situational/last-mile* source should win, so an operator can override anything at launch without rebuilding the artifact or editing files baked into the image. **Relaxed binding ties in:** `SERVER_PORT` (env) maps to `server.port` because env-var names are upper-snake-cased equivalents. **No conflict error:** Spring never fails on 'conflicts' — it deterministically picks the highest-precedence source. **Practical takeaway:** to debug 'why is my property X?', remember a higher layer is probably overriding the file.
sb-config-mcq-001.example:
```bash
# application.properties (baked into the jar)
#   server.port=8080

# Environment variable (e.g. set in the container)
export SERVER_PORT=9090

# Command-line argument at launch — HIGHEST precedence, wins
java -jar app.jar --server.port=7070
# => app binds to 7070, ignoring both 9090 and 8080

# Order (high -> low): CLI args > -D system props > env vars > profile file > application.properties
```

resources.label: Spring Boot — External Config: Property Source Order

sb-config-005.explanation: **The rule:** secrets (DB passwords, API keys, tokens) must never be committed in `application.properties`. **The technique:** keep a placeholder in the file and resolve it from a higher-precedence source at runtime — `spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}`. Because of Boot's externalized-config precedence, `${DB_PASSWORD}` is satisfied by an OS env var, a system property, or an injected secret. **Where the value actually comes from in real deployments:** OS environment, a container orchestrator secret (Kubernetes `Secret` → env var), a cloud secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager / SSM Parameter Store), HashiCorp Vault, or Spring Cloud Config (which can be encrypted). **Why this is better:** the artifact stays environment-agnostic and contains no secrets; rotating a secret is an ops action, not a code change. **Common mistake:** putting prod credentials in `application-prod.properties` and committing it — still in source control. Keep the *value* outside the repo.
sb-config-005.example:
```yaml
# application.yml — references, not literal secrets
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/app
    username: app
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}        # resolved from the environment at runtime

api:
  stripe-key: ${STRIPE_KEY:}        # empty default; required to be set in prod
```
```bash
# Supplied by the platform (k8s Secret -> env var, Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, ...)
export DB_PASSWORD='s3cr3t-from-vault'
java -jar app.jar
```

sb-web-001.explanation: **The distinction is about what the return value means.** **`@Controller`** is the classic MVC controller: a handler that returns a **view name** (a String) which a `ViewResolver` maps to a template (Thymeleaf, JSP) for server-side HTML rendering. **`@RestController`** = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody`, applied class-wide: every handler's return value is **serialized straight into the HTTP response body** — a POJO becomes JSON via Jackson, no view resolution. **When to use which:** REST/JSON APIs → `@RestController`; server-rendered HTML pages → `@Controller`. **Mixing:** inside a `@Controller` you can put `@ResponseBody` on individual methods to make just those return data instead of a view. **Status & headers:** with `@RestController` a returned object yields `200 OK`; when you need other statuses/headers, return `ResponseEntity`. **Common mistake:** using `@Controller` for an API and getting a 'no view found' error because Spring tried to resolve your JSON string as a template name.

sb-web-002.explanation: **The base:** `@RequestMapping` maps requests to handler methods by path, HTTP method, params, headers, content type, etc. **The shortcuts:** `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping`, `@PutMapping`, `@DeleteMapping`, `@PatchMapping` are composed annotations that pre-set `method = GET/POST/...` — so `@GetMapping("/users")` == `@RequestMapping(value="/users", method=RequestMethod.GET)`. **Class + method composition:** put `@RequestMapping("/api/users")` on the class to set a base path; method-level `@GetMapping("/{id}")` extends it to `/api/users/{id}`. **Why prefer the shortcuts:** more readable and they prevent the classic bug of forgetting to constrain the method (a bare `@RequestMapping` matches *all* methods). **Other useful attributes:** `produces`/`consumes` to constrain by content type, `params`/`headers` for finer matching. **Mistake to avoid:** two handlers that match the same path+method → ambiguous mapping exception at startup.

sb-web-003.explanation: **`@PathVariable`** binds a segment of the URL **path** declared as a template variable: route `/users/{id}` + `@PathVariable Long id`. It identifies *which resource*. **`@RequestParam`** binds a **query-string** parameter (or form field): `/users?active=true&page=2` + `@RequestParam boolean active`, `@RequestParam int page`. It filters/qualifies a request. **REST convention:** path variables for resource identity (`/orders/42`), query params for filtering, sorting, pagination (`/orders?status=open&page=0`). **Attributes:** `@RequestParam` supports `required` and `defaultValue` (e.g. `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page`); path variables are inherently required since they're part of the matched route. **Type conversion:** both auto-convert the String to the declared type; a bad conversion yields a 400. **Common mistake:** name mismatch — if the variable name differs from the template/param name, set it explicitly: `@PathVariable("id") Long userId`.

sb-web-004.explanation: **What it does:** `@RequestBody` on a method parameter tells Spring to take the raw HTTP **request body** and deserialize it into that object using an `HttpMessageConverter`. For JSON that's the Jackson converter; the chosen converter depends on the request's `Content-Type`. **Symmetry:** `@RequestBody` (input) mirrors `@ResponseBody` (output, serialize return value into the response body). In a `@RestController`, `@ResponseBody` is implied class-wide, so you typically only write `@RequestBody` on inputs. **Validation:** combine with `@Valid` to run Bean Validation before your handler runs — invalid input → `MethodArgumentNotValidException` → 400. **Content negotiation:** Jackson handles JSON out of the box (it's on the `-web` starter); add converters for XML, etc. **Common mistakes:** (1) forgetting `@RequestBody`, so Spring tries to bind body fields as query/form params and the object comes back empty; (2) the DTO needs a no-arg constructor / accessible fields for Jackson.

sb-web-005.explanation: **The choice:** return a plain object and Spring always responds **200 OK** with that object serialized as the body. Return **`ResponseEntity<T>`** when you must control the **status code and/or headers** too. **Common patterns:** `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing at the new resource; `404 Not Found` when a lookup misses; `204 No Content` for a successful delete; `409 Conflict`, etc. **Builders:** `ResponseEntity.ok(body)`, `ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(...)`, `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(...)`, `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()`, `ResponseEntity.noContent().build()`. **Alternative:** `@ResponseStatus` on an exception class or handler method sets the status declaratively when you don't need the full builder. **Why it matters for REST:** clients rely on accurate status codes; returning 200 for everything (even errors) is a common anti-pattern. **Generic type:** `ResponseEntity<Void>` for empty bodies; `ResponseEntity<ErrorDto>` for error payloads.

sb-web-006.explanation: **The problem:** putting try/catch in every endpoint to translate exceptions into HTTP responses is repetitive and inconsistent. **The solution:** centralize it. A class annotated `@RestControllerAdvice` (= `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`) holds `@ExceptionHandler` methods that catch exceptions thrown by *any* controller and map each to a structured response (status + body). **How it works:** when a controller throws, Spring searches the advice for an `@ExceptionHandler` matching the exception type (most specific wins) and invokes it. **Typical shape:** a handler returns a `ResponseEntity<ErrorResponse>` with the right status and a consistent error DTO (timestamp, message, field errors). **Built-in exceptions:** extend `ResponseEntityExceptionHandler` to customize Spring's own exceptions (validation `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, malformed JSON, missing params). **Scope control:** `@RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = ...)` limits which controllers it applies to. **Benefit:** one place defines the API's entire error contract.

sb-web-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer — `@PostMapping`.** It maps HTTP **POST**, the verb conventionally used to *create* a resource (submit data the server processes, often resulting in a new entity). **The others:** `@PutMapping` handles **PUT** (replace/fully update a resource at a known URI; idempotent), `@GetMapping` handles **GET** (safe, read-only retrieval), and `@RequestParam` is not a mapping at all — it binds a query/form parameter to a method argument. **POST vs PUT for create:** POST to a collection (`POST /users`) lets the server assign the id and is the usual create; PUT to a specific URI (`PUT /users/42`) is used when the client supplies the id and the operation should be idempotent. **REST convention recap:** GET=read, POST=create, PUT=replace, PATCH=partial update, DELETE=remove. **Why method-specific annotations:** they constrain the verb so the same path can have different handlers per method and you don't accidentally accept the wrong verb.

sb-web-007.explanation: **The setup:** add `spring-boot-starter-validation` (brings Hibernate Validator, the Bean Validation implementation). **On the DTO:** annotate fields with constraints — `@NotNull`, `@NotBlank`, `@Email`, `@Size(min=, max=)`, `@Min`/`@Max`, `@Pattern`, etc. **On the controller:** put `@Valid` (or `@Validated`) on the `@RequestBody` parameter so validation runs *before* your handler body. **On failure:** Spring throws `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which by default produces a 400; shape the response with a `@RestControllerAdvice` `@ExceptionHandler` to return field-level error details. **For path/query params (not a body):** put `@Validated` on the controller class and constraints directly on the parameters (`@RequestParam @Min(1) int page`). **Nested validation:** put `@Valid` on a nested object field to cascade. **Custom rules:** write a custom `ConstraintValidator` + annotation. **Common mistake:** forgetting the validation starter (annotations silently do nothing) or omitting `@Valid` (constraints aren't triggered).

resources.label: Spring — Validation, Data Binding, and Type Conversion

sb-web-mr-001.explanation: **Why 201 and 204 are the correct picks:** **201 Created** is the conventional success status for a request that creates a new resource (a successful POST), typically accompanied by a `Location` header pointing to the new resource's URI. **204 No Content** is the convention for a successful operation that returns no body (a successful DELETE, or a PUT/PATCH where you don't echo the entity). **Why the others are wrong:** a request for a missing resource should return **404 Not Found**, not 200 with an empty body (200 says 'here is the resource'); a validation failure is a client error in the **4xx** range (typically **400 Bad Request** or 422), not 500 (which signals a server fault the client can't fix); and not every success is 200 — 201/202/204 are all valid success codes. **The principle:** status codes are part of your API contract; clients branch on them, so use them accurately.

sb-web-008.explanation: **The traditional model:** you built a WAR and deployed it into a separately installed servlet container (Tomcat, WildFly). **Boot's model:** `spring-boot-starter-web` includes an **embedded** servlet container (Tomcat by default) packaged inside your application. `java -jar app.jar` starts the container in-process and begins serving — nothing external to install or deploy into. **Why this is great:** the runnable 'fat JAR' contains your code + dependencies + the server, so it runs identically on a laptop, CI, or in a minimal container image — perfect for microservices and Docker. **Swapping servers:** exclude Tomcat from the starter and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` or `spring-boot-starter-undertow`. **Configuration:** `server.port` (default 8080), `server.servlet.context-path`, thread pools, etc., via properties. **Still WAR-able:** you can still produce a WAR for legacy app servers by extending `SpringBootServletInitializer`, but the embedded fat JAR is the default and recommended path.

resources.label: Spring Boot — Creating an Executable Jar

sb-data-001.explanation: **The boilerplate it eliminates:** with raw JDBC/Hibernate you write DAO classes full of repetitive `EntityManager`/connection/query code. **What Spring Data JPA does:** you declare a **repository interface** extending `JpaRepository<Entity, IdType>`, and at runtime Spring Data generates a proxy implementing it — no hand-written class. You get `save`, `saveAll`, `findById` (→ `Optional`), `findAll`, `count`, `delete`, etc., for free. **Query methods:** add finder methods by naming convention (`findByEmail`) and it derives the query; or annotate with `@Query` for custom JPQL/SQL. **Where it sits:** on top of JPA (Hibernate as the default provider), which is on top of JDBC. **How it's wired:** Boot auto-configures the `EntityManagerFactory`, `DataSource`, and transaction manager from properties, and `@EnableJpaRepositories` (implicit in Boot) scans for repository interfaces. **Benefit:** you focus on entities + the few custom queries, not plumbing.

sb-data-002.explanation: **`@Entity`:** marks a class as a JPA persistent entity — it maps to a database table and instances map to rows. The class needs a **no-arg constructor** (JPA instantiates via reflection) and a mapped identifier. **`@Id`:** marks the primary-key field. **`@GeneratedValue`:** delegates id generation to the database/provider rather than your code. Strategies: `IDENTITY` (DB auto-increment column — most common with MySQL/Postgres serial), `SEQUENCE` (a DB sequence object — efficient batching), `TABLE` (a key table — portable but slow), `AUTO` (provider picks). **Other mapping annotations:** `@Table(name=...)` and `@Column(name=...)` override defaults; `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToOne`/etc. map relationships. **Common mistakes:** (1) using a primitive `long` id with `IDENTITY` (use the boxed `Long` so a new, unsaved entity has a null id); (2) forgetting the no-arg constructor; (3) putting business `equals`/`hashCode` on a generated id before it's assigned.

sb-data-003.explanation: **The hierarchy (narrow → wide):** `Repository<T,ID>` (marker, no methods) → `CrudRepository<T,ID>` (save, findById, findAll, delete, count) → `PagingAndSortingRepository<T,ID>` (adds `findAll(Pageable)` and `findAll(Sort)`) → `JpaRepository<T,ID>` (extends both and adds JPA-specific extras: `saveAll`, `flush`, `saveAndFlush`, `deleteAllInBatch`, `getReferenceById`, and `findAll` returning `List` rather than `Iterable`). **Which to pick:** most JPA apps extend `JpaRepository` for pagination + the richer operations. Extend a narrower interface if you want to deliberately limit the exposed API (e.g. read-only). **Note:** in recent Spring Data, `CrudRepository` and `PagingAndSortingRepository` were decoupled (PagingAndSorting no longer extends Crud), but `JpaRepository` still pulls everything together. **Custom methods:** regardless of which you extend, you add derived query methods and `@Query` methods on top. **Mistake:** reaching for native SQL when a derived method or `Pageable` would do.

sb-data-004.explanation: **The idea:** Spring Data parses the **method name** into a query at startup. The prefix (`findBy`, `readBy`, `getBy`, `queryBy`, `countBy`, `existsBy`, `deleteBy`) sets the operation; the rest names properties and conditions. **Keywords:** `And`, `Or`, `Between`, `LessThan`/`GreaterThan`, `Like`/`Containing`/`StartingWith`, `In`, `IsNull`, `True`/`False`, `IgnoreCase`, and `OrderBy...Asc/Desc`. Example: `findByLastNameAndAgeGreaterThanOrderByAgeDesc`. **Return types:** `Optional<T>` (single), `List<T>`, `Page<T>`/`Slice<T>` (with a `Pageable` param), `Stream<T>`, `long` (count), `boolean` (exists). **Validation:** names are checked at startup — a typo in a property name fails fast. **When to stop:** if the method name becomes a sentence, switch to `@Query`. **Common mistakes:** property-name typos (must match entity field names, traversing with `_` for nested), and forgetting that derived deletes/`@Modifying` queries need a transaction.

sb-data-005.explanation: **When to use `@Query`:** when a derived method name would be unwieldy, when you need joins/aggregations/projections, or when you want full control over the query. **JPQL (default):** queries the **entity model** — class and field names, not table/column names — so it's database-agnostic and refactor-friendly: `SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.email = :email`. **Native (`nativeQuery = true`):** raw **SQL** against actual tables/columns; use it for DB-specific features (window functions, vendor functions) at the cost of portability. **Parameters:** named (`:email` + `@Param("email")`) or positional (`?1`). **Modifying queries:** for UPDATE/DELETE add `@Modifying` and run in a transaction. **Projections:** select into a DTO with a constructor expression or interface-based projection. **Rule of thumb:** prefer JPQL for portability; reach for native only when JPQL can't express it. **Common mistake:** writing native SQL out of habit and losing portability/entity-mapping benefits.

sb-data-006.explanation: **What it does:** `@Transactional` declares a method (or class) to run inside a database transaction. Spring opens a transaction before the method, commits on normal return, and **rolls back on a runtime (unchecked) exception** by default. It makes multi-step DB work atomic. **The proxy mechanism (and its gotcha):** Spring implements `@Transactional` with an AOP proxy that wraps the bean. A call from *outside* goes through the proxy → transaction applied. A **self-invocation** (one method in the bean calling another `@Transactional` method via `this`) bypasses the proxy, so the annotation is silently ignored. **Other key facts:** default rollback is for `RuntimeException`/`Error` only — checked exceptions commit unless you set `rollbackFor`; the method generally must be **public** to be intercepted; place it on the **service** layer, not repositories or controllers. **Attributes:** `readOnly`, `propagation` (e.g. `REQUIRES_NEW`), `isolation`, `timeout`. **Fix for self-invocation:** move the inner method to another bean, or self-inject the proxy.

sb-data-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer — `Optional<T>`.** `CrudRepository`/`JpaRepository.findById(id)` returns `Optional<T>` so the not-found case is part of the type and you can't accidentally dereference a null. **How you use it:** `repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new ResourceNotFoundException(...))`, or `.map(...)`, `.ifPresent(...)`, `.orElse(default)`. **Why not null:** returning null invites `NullPointerException` and hides the 'might be absent' contract; `Optional` makes it explicit and composable. **The alternative when you *want* an exception:** `getReferenceById(id)` (formerly `getOne`) returns a lazy proxy and throws when accessed if absent — handy when you only need a reference for an association, not the loaded entity. **Distractor traps:** it does *not* return a bare `T` or null, does not throw by itself, and returns a single `Optional`, not a `List`. **Practical tip:** pair `findById` with `.orElseThrow` in a service and let a `@RestControllerAdvice` turn that exception into a 404.

sb-data-007.explanation: **What N+1 is:** you run **1** query to load N parent rows, then touching a **lazy** association on each parent fires **1 more query per parent** — total 1 + N queries. With 100 parents that's 101 round-trips, killing performance. **Why it happens:** JPA associations default to LAZY (for `@OneToMany`) — a good default (don't load what you don't use) — but iterating parents and accessing the lazy collection in a loop triggers a query each time. **Fixes (per query, not global):** (1) **`JOIN FETCH`** in JPQL — `SELECT p FROM Post p JOIN FETCH p.comments` loads parents + children in one query; (2) **`@EntityGraph`** on the repository method — declaratively eager-fetch named attributes; (3) **batch fetching** — `@BatchSize`/`hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` turns N selects into a few `IN (...)` selects. **What NOT to do:** flip the association to `FetchType.EAGER` globally — that over-fetches everywhere and just moves the problem. **Detect it:** enable SQL logging (`spring.jpa.show-sql=true`) or use a tool like Hibernate statistics / datasource-proxy and watch for repeated identical selects.

sb-test-001.explanation: **What it does:** `@SpringBootTest` bootstraps the **entire application context** — the same bean graph as production — for an integration test. **When it's right:** end-to-end behavior spanning multiple layers (controller → service → repository), wiring/configuration correctness, or anything needing the full context. **When it's the WRONG choice:** testing a single slice. Booting the whole context is slow; if you only exercise a controller, use `@WebMvcTest`; only a repository, use `@DataJpaTest`; pure logic with no Spring, just `new` the class with mocks — no context at all. **Web testing modes:** `webEnvironment = MOCK` (default, no real server, use `MockMvc`) or `RANDOM_PORT`/`DEFINED_PORT` (real embedded server, use `TestRestTemplate`/`WebTestClient` for actual HTTP). **Speed tips:** Spring caches contexts between tests with identical configuration — avoid gratuitously different `@MockBean`/property combos that fragment the cache. **Common mistake:** defaulting every test to `@SpringBootTest` and ending up with a slow suite that could mostly be slice or unit tests.

sb-test-002.explanation: **What it loads:** `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)` boots only the **web slice** — the named controller, `@ControllerAdvice`, JSON converters (Jackson), validation, filters, `MockMvc` — but **not** services, repositories, or the full context. **Why:** it's fast and focused on web concerns: routing, parameter binding, deserialization/serialization, validation, status codes, exception handling. **`MockMvc`:** lets you perform fake HTTP requests in-process (no running server) and assert on the response — status, headers, JSON body (with `jsonPath`). **Collaborators:** the controller's dependencies (services) aren't in this slice, so you supply them as `@MockBean`s and stub their behavior. **What it's NOT for:** testing service logic or real persistence — those need their own tests. **Common mistakes:** forgetting to `@MockBean` a service the controller needs (context fails to load), or asserting business rules here that actually live in the (mocked-away) service. **Security note:** if Spring Security is on the classpath, `@WebMvcTest` applies it — use `@WithMockUser` or test config to authenticate.

sb-test-003.explanation: **What it does:** `@MockBean` creates a Mockito mock and registers it in the Spring test context, **replacing** any existing bean of the same type. The component under test then receives the mock via normal injection. You stub it with `when(...).thenReturn(...)` and verify interactions with `verify(...)`. **Why it exists (vs plain `@Mock`):** `@Mock` (with Mockito alone) gives you a mock object but doesn't put it in a Spring context — fine for pure unit tests built with `new`. `@MockBean` is for tests that *do* spin up a context (`@WebMvcTest`, `@SpringBootTest`) where Spring must inject the dependency. **Best fit:** slice tests (mock the service behind a controller) and integration tests where you want to stub an external system (payment gateway, email) while keeping the rest real. **Caution:** each distinct `@MockBean` setup creates a new context (cache fragmentation → slower suite); and overusing it inside `@SpringBootTest` undermines the point of an integration test. **Note:** in newer Spring Boot, `@MockitoBean` is the successor annotation.

resources.label: Spring Boot — Mocking and Spying Beans (@MockBean)

sb-test-004.explanation: **What it loads:** `@DataJpaTest` boots only the **persistence slice** — entities, Spring Data repositories, an `EntityManager`/`TestEntityManager`, and the JPA infrastructure — not controllers or services. **Test database:** by default it replaces your configured `DataSource` with an **in-memory embedded database** (H2/HSQLDB/Derby if on the classpath), so tests are fast and don't touch real data. **Transactions:** each test method runs in a transaction that is **rolled back** at the end, so tests are isolated and leave no residue. **What it's for:** verifying repository queries — derived methods, `@Query`, mappings, constraints — against a real (if in-memory) database. **`TestEntityManager`:** persist/flush fixtures and clear the persistence context to test fresh reads. **Override the DB:** `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)` keeps your real datasource (e.g. to test against Postgres via Testcontainers) — important because some queries behave differently across databases. **Common mistake:** trusting H2 to mirror prod SQL exactly (native queries/vendor features can differ).

resources.label: Spring Boot — Auto-configured Data JPA Tests (@DataJpaTest)

sb-test-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer — `@WebMvcTest`.** The requirement is narrow: one controller's request mapping + JSON serialization, *fast*, *no services or DB*. That's exactly a web slice test — `@WebMvcTest` loads only the MVC layer and gives you `MockMvc` to fire requests and assert status/JSON. Collaborators are provided as `@MockBean`. **Why the others are wrong:** **`@SpringBootTest`** boots the *entire* context (services, repositories, datasource) — correct for end-to-end integration but slow and overkill for one controller. **`@DataJpaTest`** is the *persistence* slice (repositories + in-memory DB) — wrong layer entirely. **`@Component`** isn't a test annotation; it registers a bean. **The general principle — slice tests:** Spring Boot offers focused slices (`@WebMvcTest`, `@DataJpaTest`, `@JsonTest`, `@RestClientTest`, …) so you load only what a test needs. Reserve `@SpringBootTest` for genuine cross-layer integration tests, and use plain JUnit + Mockito (no context) for pure logic.

sb-actuator-001.explanation: **What it is:** Spring Boot Actuator is the **production/operations** module — add `spring-boot-starter-actuator` and you get a set of management endpoints for monitoring and introspecting a running app, exposed over HTTP (under `/actuator`) and/or JMX. **Key endpoints:** `health` (UP/DOWN + component checks), `info` (build/app metadata), `metrics` (JVM, HTTP, custom — backed by Micrometer, exportable to Prometheus/Datadog/etc.), `env` (resolved config), `loggers` (view/change log levels at runtime), `threaddump`, `heapdump`, `mappings`, `beans`. **Who uses it:** load balancers/orchestrators poll `health` for liveness/readiness; monitoring systems scrape `metrics`; on-call engineers inspect `env`/`loggers`/`threaddump` during incidents. **Security caution:** many endpoints expose sensitive internals, so only `health` is web-exposed by default — you opt others in and secure them. **Extensibility:** add custom `HealthIndicator`s, `info` contributors, and Micrometer metrics. **The value:** observability and runtime management without writing the plumbing yourself.
sb-actuator-001.example:
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
```
```properties
# application.properties — expose a curated, safe set over HTTP
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,loggers
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
# Then: GET /actuator/health, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used ...
```

sb-actuator-002.explanation: **What it reports:** `/actuator/health` aggregates the status of the app and its critical dependencies into one overall `UP` or `DOWN` (also `OUT_OF_SERVICE`, `UNKNOWN`). Boot auto-registers indicators for things on the classpath — `db` (a test query), `diskSpace`, `redis`, `mongo`, message brokers, etc. **Who consumes it:** load balancers and orchestrators use it as a probe: if it's DOWN, stop routing traffic / restart the instance. **Detail visibility:** by default it shows only the overall status (to avoid leaking internals); set `management.endpoint.health.show-details=always` (or `when-authorized`) to see per-component breakdowns. **Kubernetes probes:** Boot supports **liveness** and **readiness** groups (`/actuator/health/liveness`, `/actuator/health/readiness`) — liveness failing → restart the pod; readiness failing → temporarily remove from the service. **Custom checks:** implement `HealthIndicator` (or `ReactiveHealthIndicator`) to add app-specific checks (e.g. a downstream API). **Common mistake:** exposing full details publicly (reveals infrastructure) or making the health check itself heavy/slow.

sb-actuator-003.explanation: **Why hidden by default:** several Actuator endpoints expose sensitive data — `env` (config, possibly resolved secrets), `beans`, `configprops`, `heapdump`, `threaddump`, `mappings`. Exposing them openly would be an information-disclosure risk. So over HTTP, **only `health` is exposed by default** (JMX historically exposed more, but web is locked down). **How to expose more:** `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics` (comma list) — or `*` for all, which you should pair with security. You can also `exclude` specific ones. **Securing them:** put `/actuator/**` behind authentication via Spring Security, restrict by network/firewall, or move them to a **separate management port** (`management.server.port=9001`) that isn't publicly routable. **Change the base path:** `management.endpoints.web.base-path=/manage`. **The principle — least exposure:** expose the minimal set you actually monitor, and never blanket-`*` an internet-facing interface without auth. **Common mistake:** setting `include=*` in production with no security and leaking config via `/actuator/env`.
sb-actuator-003.example:
```properties
# Expose only what you monitor, and secure it.
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=env,beans,heapdump

# Option: isolate management on a separate, non-public port
management.server.port=9001
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/manage   # -> /manage/health

# Show health details only to authenticated users
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
```

sb-actuator-mcq-001.explanation: **The answer — `spring-boot-starter-actuator`.** It pulls in the Actuator module that provides the management endpoints (`health`, `info`, `metrics`, etc.) and auto-configures them. **Why the others don't:** **`spring-boot-starter-web`** provides Spring MVC and the embedded server — Actuator endpoints *ride over* the web layer, but the starter itself doesn't add them. **`spring-boot-starter-data-jpa`** adds JPA/Hibernate persistence (it does contribute a `db` health indicator *once* Actuator is present, but it doesn't enable Actuator). **`spring-boot-devtools`** adds development-time conveniences (automatic restart, live reload, sensible dev defaults) — nothing to do with production endpoints. **Practical recap:** add `starter-actuator`, then choose what to expose with `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`, and secure it. Metrics integrate with Micrometer, so pair with e.g. `micrometer-registry-prometheus` to export to Prometheus.
sb-actuator-mcq-001.example:
```xml
<!-- The dependency that enables /actuator/* endpoints -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>

<!-- Optional: export metrics to Prometheus -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
    <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
    <scope>runtime</scope>
</dependency>
```

sb-sec-001.explanation: **What happens immediately:** dropping `spring-boot-starter-security` onto the classpath triggers Spring Security auto-configuration, which is **secure by default** — every endpoint now requires authentication. **The defaults you get:** HTTP Basic auth + a generated form-login page; a single in-memory user named **`user`** with a **random password printed to the console** at startup; CSRF protection enabled (for browser/form flows); and secure response headers (X-Content-Type-Options, cache-control, etc.). **Why 'secure by default':** the framework would rather lock everything down and make you *consciously open* what should be public than ship something accidentally exposed. **What you do next:** define a `SecurityFilterChain` to permit your public endpoints (`/`, `/login`, static assets, health), choose a real authentication mechanism (form login, OAuth2/JWT), and replace the in-memory user with a real `UserDetailsService` / user store. **Common surprises:** an API suddenly returns 401, or POSTs fail with 403 because CSRF is on (for stateless APIs you typically disable CSRF and use tokens). The console password is for bootstrapping only.

sb-sec-002.explanation: **The modern approach — component-based config:** define one or more `SecurityFilterChain` **beans** in a `@Configuration` class. Each configures an `HttpSecurity` and returns the built chain. This replaced the old `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter` subclassing, which was **deprecated and removed in Spring Security 6**. **What you configure on `HttpSecurity` (lambda DSL):** request authorization (`authorizeHttpRequests`), the login mechanism (`formLogin`, `httpBasic`, `oauth2ResourceServer`), CSRF, CORS, session management (e.g. `STATELESS` for token APIs), headers. **Authorization rules:** `requestMatchers("/public/**").permitAll()`, `requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`, then `anyRequest().authenticated()` as a catch-all — order matters; first match wins. **For stateless REST/JWT:** typically disable CSRF, set session creation to STATELESS, and add `oauth2ResourceServer(jwt)`. **Method security:** enable `@EnableMethodSecurity` to use `@PreAuthorize` on services. **Common mistakes:** rule ordering (broad rule before specific), forgetting `anyRequest()`, or leaving CSRF on for a stateless API (causing 403s).

sb-sec-003.explanation: **Authentication (AuthN) = who you are.** It validates credentials (password, token, certificate) and, on success, produces an `Authentication` object stored in the `SecurityContext` for the request. Handled by an `AuthenticationManager` delegating to `AuthenticationProvider`s (e.g. a `DaoAuthenticationProvider` checking a `UserDetailsService` + `PasswordEncoder`, or a JWT decoder for resource servers). **Authorization (AuthZ) = what you may do.** Given an authenticated principal and its granted authorities/roles, it decides whether a particular action is allowed. Enforced two ways in Spring Security: **request-level** rules in the `SecurityFilterChain` (`requestMatchers(...).hasRole(...)`) and **method-level** annotations (`@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")`, `@PostAuthorize`, `@Secured`) when `@EnableMethodSecurity` is on. **Order:** AuthN happens first; AuthZ uses its result — you can't authorize an unknown principal. **Roles vs authorities:** a 'role' is just an authority conventionally prefixed `ROLE_`; `hasRole("ADMIN")` checks authority `ROLE_ADMIN`. **Common confusion:** a 401 (Unauthorized) means *not authenticated*; a 403 (Forbidden) means *authenticated but not permitted* — i.e. AuthN vs AuthZ failure respectively.

sb-sec-004.explanation: **The rule:** never store passwords in plaintext (or with fast/unsalted hashes like MD5/SHA-1). A leaked database must not reveal usable passwords. **What `PasswordEncoder` does:** it one-way **hashes** a raw password for storage and later **matches** a raw login attempt against the stored hash. The recommended implementation is **`BCryptPasswordEncoder`** — it salts automatically and is deliberately slow (configurable work/strength factor), so brute-forcing is expensive even with leaked hashes. Alternatives: `Argon2`, `SCrypt`, `PBKDF2`. **`DelegatingPasswordEncoder`:** the default from `PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()` stores an algorithm id prefix like `{bcrypt}` in the hash, so you can **migrate algorithms over time** — old `{bcrypt}` hashes still verify while new ones use a newer scheme. **How it's used:** expose a `PasswordEncoder` bean; encode on registration (`encoder.encode(raw)`); Spring Security's `DaoAuthenticationProvider` uses it to verify logins via `matches`. **Common mistakes:** storing plaintext, comparing with `==`/`equals` instead of `matches`, using a fast hash, or hard-coding a tiny BCrypt strength.
